title: By Hand — The Maker Behind the Badge

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the thirtieth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
[wry] The spine this weekend is a quiet one, Theo. Who actually made the thing.
[curious] Meaning?
The maker behind the badge. A frame that shares a factory with a dozen designer logos. A watch worth its price only because someone restored it by hand. A drone you solder yourself.
[warmly] And a whole country that's started copying its books out by hand. I love it already. Give me the three headlines.
One. Washington opens a named economic war to force the Strait of Hormuz open — and Tehran sends back a bill.
Two. The biggest open model of the year drops its weights, then attaches a licence deciding who's allowed to run them.
And three — down the rabbit hole, first-person-view drones. The one flying machine you build yourself.
[excited] The soldering iron one. Yes. But start us with the hard news.
So. The Strait of Hormuz has now been shut to routine traffic for about a hundred and eighty days. The longest closure of the world's oil chokepoint on record.
[thoughtful] Half a year. And this week the story stopped being threats.

It did. After a Sunday-night promise of, quote, an economic D-Day, the US Treasury secretary unveiled a named sanctions campaign — aimed not just at Iran, but at the third-country buyers, banks and shippers keeping it solvent.
A codename. Which is the tell — a codename says permanence. This is a policy, not a tweet.
[deadpan] Whether it moves a single tanker is another matter. Because Iran didn't answer with a key. It answered with a list.
What's on the list?
Lift the blockade. Pay war-damage compensation. Unfreeze the economy. End the war. Maximalist by design — leverage banked for talks that haven't started.
And there's a corridor, isn't there? A way through.
Tehran and Muscat have drawn a safe-transit lane through Omani water. Oil slipped to a two-week low when it surfaced. But — the lane is charted, not sailed. No convoy has used it.
[skeptical] So two accounts of the same sea. Washington says the strait is already open; the water says about a tenth of normal traffic is moving.

Here's the sceptic line, and it's the one to hold. A campaign aimed at buyers and banks hardens Iran's stance at least as fast as it bites. And China — Iran's main customer — has already said it won't comply.
So the thing to watch isn't the press conference.
It's the first ship that actually sails the corridor. Until then, it's rhetoric on both sides.
[exhales] Right. And quickly, the region — because the map of leisure and the map of risk keep sharing coordinates.

Three navies drill off Jeju in early September. A Himalayan glacial flood has passed six hundred dead, with a second flood now threatening behind the debris. And Beijing and Washington are booking a tariff and a summit into the same fortnight.
Deterrence and diplomacy on one calendar. Grim. Take me to the money.
The money is a repricing, and it runs one way. A hawkish new Fed chair said there's, quote, work to do on inflation. Then a hot July inflation print landed.
And the market did what?
Flipped. From expecting a September hold or cut, to a coin-flip on an outright rate rise. Hike odds climbed toward the mid-fifties, per cent.
[gasps] A hike? This late? That's the opposite of where the year was pointing.
It is. Higher-for-longer stopped being a slogan and became a live tail. The dollar firmed, front-end yields firmed.
So what does that mean for the things people actually hold — an all-world index, some global bonds?
A mild headwind for both. Rising yields drag on bond prices, and firmer real yields thin the air for long-duration equities.
And gold? I thought a strong dollar was bad for gold.

[curious] It usually is. And here's the odd part — gold held within a whisker of its record, around four thousand six hundred US dollars, even as the dollar rose. The haven and central-bank demand is, for now, outmuscling the gravity that normally pulls it down.
While bitcoin?
Sagged toward eighty thousand US dollars, trading like the risk asset it is. Same force, two opposite prices. That's the whole reason to watch both.
[thoughtful] And this is explanation, not advice.
Always. Now — Singapore, because that repricing lands on a bill here.
The factories, right? They grew again.

They did — manufacturing output up six point eight per cent on the year. But read the breakdown and it narrows fast. It's almost all electronics — the same AI-chip cycle — and even that cooled to an eleven-month low.
And everything else?
Going backwards. Biomedical down, chemicals down harder. One narrow, cyclical cluster is doing the work of a whole economy's growth line.
[exhales] Which is fine while the cycle runs.

And precarious the moment it turns. The comfort this week — cost-of-living payouts of four to six hundred dollars a head land in September. The catch — they smooth a month; they don't diversify an economy.
[curious] Speaking of chips — there's a challenger, isn't there?

There is. OpenAI benchmarked its first in-house inference chip this week. Codename Jalapeño. And the numbers, from one analytics house, claim it does between one-and-a-half and nearly two times the useful work of a competing Nvidia part.
Aimed at the crown?

Aimed at the fattest part of the crown — inference, serving the models. That's the highest-margin slice. When you're the world's biggest renter of someone else's silicon, building your own is how you stop paying rent.
[skeptical] But one analytics house. And tiny volumes.

Exactly the sceptic line. The volumes are tiny, and OpenAI says it'll keep buying Nvidia by the boatload. Nvidia just printed a ninety-six-billion-dollar quarter. Custom silicon narrowing a margin isn't the same as unseating a platform.
And the home-lab crowd got a big one too.

They did — and it comes with strings. Zhipu dropped the full weights of its flagship model, G L M five point three. Seven hundred and forty-four billion parameters. Reversing a hold they'd placed over cyber-misuse fears.
Open weights! That's the good news.
[wry] Read the licence. Any provider clearing ten billion US dollars of revenue has to pass Zhipu's own security review first. It's the first time the newest open model comes with a permission slip.
Ah. And could I even run it at home?

Not a chance. Four hundred and forty-five gigabytes of memory at four-bit — that's a data-centre, not a study. The one that matters for a home rig is the smaller Flash model, which stays genuinely open.
[amused] Read the licence, not the parameter count. Okay — the Kit. The glasses everyone's talking about.
RayNeo's iO. On sale next week, four hundred and seventy-nine US dollars. And its best feature is a deletion.
A deletion?

No camera. On purpose. In a category defined by pointing a lens at people, they left the lens out and kept a little green display floating in the right lens. The bet is that the heads-up display is the part worth wearing.
[warmly] I actually love that. Restraint as a feature.
[deadpan] The sceptic's note — camera-free is not data-free. It's still an always-on microphone on your face, and nobody's lived with a shipping unit yet. First impressions only.
And the Atelier — this is the eyewear one, the maker-behind-the-badge thesis in its purest form.

The purest. Here's the mechanism. A quality frame is cut from cellulose acetate — colour running all the way through, hand-polished over days at the Japanese benches in Sabae. A cheap one is injection-moulded plastic with the colour sprayed on.
And the hinge, you said, is the tell.

Count the barrels, or buy no screw at all. But the real story is the white-label truth. One company — EssilorLuxottica — owns Ray-Ban, Oakley, Persol, and also prints, for a royalty, Chanel, Prada, Versace and Burberry.
[gasps] So the Prada frame and the Versace frame —

Come off the same line. A designer logo is largely brand tax. Functional quality is essentially maxed by the Japanese sweet spot, around three to seven hundred US dollars. Buy the maker, not the badge.
[excited] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every weekend with this line.
[laughs] First-person-view drones, Claire. Tell me the difference from the camera drone in my drawer.

Night and day. A camera drone flies itself — it hovers, it comes home at the tap of a button. A true F-P-V quad, in manual mode, has no self-levelling and no hover. The throttle is raw thrust. It drops the instant you stop flying it.
So you're not watching a screen —
You're wearing goggles fed a live camera feed from the nose. You are, in every sense that matters, inside the aircraft. That's the gateway drug and the skill ceiling at once.
[curious] How big is this world?
The market's around one-and-a-half billion US dollars. The racing league alone has some thirty-eight thousand members. And the culture is that people still solder their own machines.
Okay, I'm a beginner with a buy-once budget. Where does the money go?

[thoughtful] Here's the counterintuitive part. Don't spend on the aircraft. The quad is a consumable — you will crash it, repeatedly, on purpose. Spend on the two things that survive every crash: the radio and the goggles.
Because those transfer to every future build.
Exactly. The control link, the goggles — buy those once and well. Everything strapped to the frame is priced to be replaced, and the market is designed to sell you the next one.
And what's genuinely new this year?

A sharper high-definition air unit from D-J-I, a control link that finally does long-range rescue natively, and a palm-sized drone with all-round sensing. Real steps, the community agrees — not just new box art.
[amused] And can I even fly it here? Singapore's not exactly open sky.

[wry] It is not. Anything over two hundred and fifty grams must be registered. Flight's capped low, banned within five kilometres of any airfield — which is most of the island — and flying under goggles legally needs a spotter watching the craft.
So realistically?

Realistically, it's a tiny sub-two-hundred-and-fifty-gram machine, flown indoors or at the club fields, with a simulator doing the early learning. A twenty-dollar sim that saves hundreds in crashed hardware.
[laughs] And the honest sceptic line?

It's a subscription of parts and power. A hundred to three hundred US dollars a year, minimum. The endgame build is a myth — there's always a new air unit. What you're really buying is a skill nothing else replicates.
[warmly] That's the good stuff. What's tomorrow's rabbit hole?
Reader's choice. Tenkara — fixed-line fly fishing. Home mixology. Or vinyl and turntables.
[curious] Culture desk — and there's a lovely one this week. The cartoon that came back from the dead.
Coyote versus Acme. A finished film its studio shelved in twenty twenty-three for a tax write-off — valued more deleted than released.
[gasps] They tried to erase it?

They did. A public campaign and a small distributor pulled it back. It opened this weekend — a modest fourteen million US dollars or so, third place, but the critics have it certified fresh in the mid-nineties.
So the box office is the footnote.
That it survived at all is the point. The fans won, even if the box office didn't.
[warmly] And the watch — this one's the spine again, isn't it. Provenance on the wrist.
The Singer Reimagined Heritage V seventy-two. It takes a genuine, unused nineteen-seventies chronograph movement, restores it by hand, and engraves the bridge, quote, Restored by Singer.
So you're buying the hand that saved it.

[thoughtful] You are. And it's honest about the trade. Twenty-three thousand Swiss francs for a restored movement that a modern automatic beats on every spec. The value is the restoration and the finishing — not the rate.
Quick one for the parents, because I know they're listening.

A large study links heavy screen use in kids to worse mental health. But the useful finding is why — it runs through sleep and lost activity. So the lever isn't a screen ban. It's protecting the bedtime and the daily movement.
[warmly] Guard the sleep, not the minutes. And it lands the same term Singapore's schools put phones away.
Exactly the term a twelve-year-old starts secondary school. General guidance, not medical advice.
And one for the body — the lazy person's win, I hope.
[amused] Sort of. A new analysis finds that piling on sprint repetitions doesn't add to the aerobic payoff. A few all-out efforts buy about the same lungs as a punishing session.
So fewer sprints, same result?

With a caveat — the studies lean on young, already-fit subjects. And the honest doctor's line is that adherence beats protocol. The easy base you'll actually keep doing beats the perfect session you quit. Not medical advice.
[curious] Before we go slow — one for the travellers, because it's a weekend.
Two things. If you're shopping in Japan this autumn, the tax-free rules flip on the first of November. You pay the full price at the till now, and claim the refund at the airport before you fly.
So budget the extra queue.
Budget the queue. And this weekend's Grand Tour is the Seto Inland Sea art islands — Naoshima and its neighbours.
[warmly] The Tadao Ando ones. Art you go to by the maker's name.

The spine again. A Monet room lit only by the sky. A water-drop pavilion the forums quietly rate above everything else. And Kusama's yellow pumpkin on a pier — once washed out to sea by a typhoon, and rebuilt ten per cent thicker to stand again.
One piece of advice?

Stay overnight. The day-trippers get the crowded midday version; the traveller who sleeps on the island gets the pumpkin at dawn. And this isn't a festival year, so the art is all open with thinner crowds.
[thoughtful] And the long read. Take us out slow.
This one's from Korea. In the most wired country on earth, a generation is spending its evenings copying novels into notebooks — by hand, in silence, for an hour at a time.
[curious] Copying? By hand? Why?

They call it pilsa. Once a study drill; now a movement. Sales of the books made for it jumped nearly seven hundred per cent in a year. And here's the striking part — people in their twenties are the only age group in Korea whose reading is rising.
[warmly] While everyone else's falls.

While everyone else's falls. And it's not nostalgia. It descends from Buddhist sutra-copying — a centuries-old contemplative practice, back as a product, at the exact moment a machine learned to write for free.
So it's a reaction to the AI.

[drawn out] It's the counter-movement. The same twenty-somethings who made a chatbot their search engine are the ones sitting in silence, copying by hand. They're not rejecting the machine. They're drawing a line around the one thing they won't hand it.
Which is?
The authorship of their own attention. When a machine can write anything on demand, the scarce thing stops being information — and becomes proof that a human mind spent the time.
[thoughtful] The hand is the cutting edge of the mind.
Bronowski's line. The whole issue in six words. The badge is easy to buy. The hand is the part you can't outsource.
[warmly] And Korea got there first —
Because Korea is furthest in. When the big Western papers write it up in a few weeks, we'll have told you first. That's the whole point of the desk.
[exhales] What a place to end.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
